# **IEAP-Rstudio-Series03**

### Data wrangling and ANOVA

# **1 ANOVA: Analysis of variance**

### 1.1 **Think before coding**

The scientific question is:

**Is the effect of difficulty on Movement Time the same across all groups?**

More specifically, we aim to investigate how the effect of the Index of Difficulty (ID) on Movement Time differs between the three groups: stroke patients, age-matched controls, and young controls.

We hypothesize that the effect of difficulty on Movement Time is stronger in the post-stroke patient group than in the two control groups.

**How do we visualize this?**

We use graphs created with `ggplot2` in R to plot Movement Time against the Index of Difficulty for each group. The regression lines allow us to compare the relationship between difficulty and Movement Time across groups.

**Is there a significant difference?**

We use an ANOVA to test whether the effect of difficulty on Movement Time differs between groups. The significance threshold is set at α = 0.01.

**What conclusion can we draw?**

The ANOVA revealed a significant GROUP × ID interaction (F (2, 48) = 11.58, p < 0.01), indicating that the effect of difficulty on Movement Time differs significantly between the three groups. As shown in the graph, Movement Time increases with difficulty in all three groups, but this increase is much stronger in the post stroke patients’ group than in the two control groups.

## **1.2 What library to answer the above questions?**

### Load library

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ez)
```

## **1.3 Data reorganization**

## Load data

```{r}
data <- read.table(
  text = readLines("data/Results.txt"),
  header = TRUE,
  sep = "",
  stringsAsFactors = TRUE
)

head(data)
```

We need to reorganize the data.

To do so, we count the number of data points for each combination of factors to check if there is missing data.

The following function looks for every unique combination of GROUP and ID in the dataset and tallies up the number of rows for each pair. It automatically generates a new column named n that contains these totals. we do that to check if the number of rows is the same for every combination.

```{r}
data_counts <- data %>%
  count(GROUP, ID)

print(data_counts)
```

For item 9 "pp ID3 400", the number of rows does not match the rest of the group 'PP', so we need to delete ID3. The fact that some data are missing is explained by some stroke patients not being able to perform the test at ID3.

```{r}
data %>%
  filter(ID != "ID3") %>%
  count(GROUP, ID)

```

Now let's look at other columns such as REP.

```{r }
data %>% 
  filter(ID != "ID3") %>%
  count(REP)
```

The number of repetitions for R3 is half the number of R1 and R2. Therefore, we delete R3 data from our data frame.

```{r}

data %>% 
  filter(ID != "ID3") %>%
  filter(REP != "R3") %>%
  count(GROUP, ID, REP)
```

We created a tibble 3 × 2 to look for the number of participants in each group.

```{r}
data %>% 
  filter(ID != "ID3") %>%
  filter(REP != "R3") %>%
  distinct(GROUP, SUBJ) %>%
  count(GROUP, name='count')
```

Now we create a new variable to store the cleaned data.

```{r}
data_clean <- data %>% 
  filter(ID != "ID3") %>% 
  filter(REP != "R3")
head(data_clean)
```

# 1.7 Discuss the differences with the article

Our results may differ slightly from those reported in the article because we used a simpler analysis method.

First, we excluded observations corresponding to ID3 and repetition R3 during data cleaning. Second, we fitted separate linear regressions for each group using the trials pooled across participants, rather than fitting a separate regression for each participant. Finally, we represented variability using error bars corresponding to ±0.5 standard deviations.

Despite these methodological differences, our results are consistent with the main conclusion of the article. Movement Time increases with the Index of Difficulty in all three groups, but the increase is much stronger in the post-stroke patient group (pp; slope ≈ 0.90 s/bit) than in the two control groups (ap and cp; slopes ≈ 0.17 and 0.12 s/bit, respectively). The significant GROUP × ID interaction in the ANOVA supports the conclusion that the effect of difficulty differs between groups.

However, our analysis has limitations. In particular, using only two difficulty levels does not allow us to assess the linearity of the relationship over a wider range of difficulty levels. Moreover, pooling trials across participants does not account for individual differences in the regression slopes. Therefore, although our results support a similar overall interpretation, they should not be considered an exact replication of the analysis presented in the article.

# Data sources and references

### Data source

- `Results.txt`: movement time data from a Fitts' pointing task performed by three groups of participants (ap, cp, pp), provided by Denis Mottet for the IEAP RStudio course. Available at: <https://moodle.umontpellier.fr/course/view.php?id=41022>

### Scientific references

- Mottet, D., van Dokkum, L. E. H., Froger, J., Gouaïch, A., & Laffont, I. (2017). Trajectory formation principles are the same after mild or moderate stroke. *PLoS ONE*, 12(3), e0173674. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0173674>
- Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. *Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 47(6), 381–391. <https://doi.org/10.1037/h0055392>

### Software and R packages

- R Core Team (2025). *R: A language and environment for statistical computing*. R Foundation for Statistical Computing. <https://www.R-project.org/>
- Wickham, H., et al. (2019). Welcome to the tidyverse. *Journal of Open Source Software*, 4(43), 1686. <https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.01686>
- Lawrence, M. A. *ez: Easy analysis and visualization of factorial experiments*. R package. <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ez>
- Müller, K. *here: A simpler way to find your files*. R package. <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=here>
